text: Two acronyms do almost all the real work in disaster recovery planning, and they get confused constantly: RTO and RPO. Get them backwards and you end up building the wrong thing — paying for continuous replication you didn't need, or discovering during an actual outage that the backup job you trusted loses far more data than the business can tolerate.

RTO, Recovery Time Objective, answers how long a system can be down before the impact is unacceptable. RPO, Recovery Point Objective, answers something different entirely: how much data can we afford to lose, measured as time since the last good copy. A system can have a tight RTO and a loose RPO, or the reverse — a financial ledger that tolerates some downtime but never a gap in its transaction history is exactly that second case.

Once a workload has a real RPO number, the backup strategy follows almost mechanically. Twenty-four hours of tolerable loss means a nightly job is genuinely enough. One hour means you need hourly incremental backups or log shipping. Seconds, or zero, means only continuous, often synchronous, replication will do — the secondary copy has to update as writes happen, not on a schedule.

RTO drives a different decision: how much infrastructure has to already exist, ready to take traffic, versus how much can be rebuilt afterward. An RTO measured in days lets you restore from backup and rebuild from Infrastructure as Code after the fact — no standing cost. An RTO under an hour usually needs a warm standby, running at reduced capacity until failover. An RTO of minutes needs a hot standby, already at full capacity, which you pay for the entire time it sits waiting.

That ordering matters. Picking a pattern like active-active because it sounds more resilient, and only afterward discovering what it costs, is backwards. The right order is the business setting RTO and RPO per workload tier first — the payments ledger does not need the same targets as the internal wiki — and the architecture being whatever combination of backup frequency and standby capacity actually satisfies those numbers.

With real RTO and RPO targets in hand for a given workload, the next question is mechanical: which multi-region pattern actually delivers them, and at what cost. That's exactly where active-active and active-passive come in, and it's the entire subject of the next lesson.
